“Well, then,” he continued, evidently making an effort to speak coherently. “I do not know how long I have loved her. But she alone, she alone, is the one I have loved all my life, and I love her so much that without her I cannot imagine life for myself. I do not dare ask for her hand now; but the thought that perhaps she might be mine and that I shall miss this chance... this chance... is terrible. Tell me, may I hope? Tell me, what am I to do? Dear Princess,” he said after a short silence, touching her hand, since she did not answer.

“I am thinking about what you have told me,” replied Princess Marya. “This is what I will say to you. You are right that to speak to her of love now...” The princess stopped. She had wanted to say that to speak to her of love now was impossible; but she stopped because for three days she had seen, from Natasha’s sudden transformation, that not only would Natasha not be offended if Pierre declared his love to her, but that this was the one thing she desired.

“To speak to her now... is impossible,” Princess Marya nevertheless said.

“But what am I to do?”

“Entrust it to me,” said Princess Marya. “I know...”

Pierre looked into Princess Marya’s eyes.

“Well, well...” he said.

“I know that she loves... will come to love you,” Princess Marya corrected herself.

No sooner had she said these words than Pierre sprang up and, with a frightened look, seized Princess Marya by the hand.

“Why do you think so? You think I may hope? You think so?!...”

“Yes, I do,” Princess Marya said with a smile. “Write to your parents. And entrust it to me. I will tell her when it is possible. I desire it. And my heart feels that it will be so.”

“No, that cannot be! How happy I am! But it cannot be... How happy I am! No, it cannot be!” Pierre kept saying, kissing Princess Marya’s hands.

“You should go to Petersburg; that is better. And I will write to you,” she said.

“To Petersburg? Go? Yes, all right, I’ll go. But may I come to see you tomorrow?”

The next day Pierre came to say goodbye. Natasha was less animated than on the preceding days; but that day, whenever he looked into her eyes, Pierre felt that he was vanishing, that neither he nor she existed any longer, but only a single feeling of happiness. “Can it really be? No, it cannot be,” he said to himself at every glance, gesture, and word of hers that filled his soul with joy.

When, as he said goodbye to her, he took her slender, thin hand, he involuntarily held it in his own a little longer.

“Can it really be that this hand, this face, these eyes, all this treasure of feminine loveliness that is foreign to me—can all this be mine forever, familiar to me, just as I am to myself? No, it is impossible!...”

“Goodbye, Count,” she said to him aloud. “I shall be waiting for you very much,” she added in a whisper.

And for two months these simple words, and the look and expression that accompanied them, formed the subject of Pierre’s inexhaustible recollections, interpretations, and happy dreams. “‘I shall be waiting for you very much’... Yes, yes, how did she say it? Yes, ‘I shall be waiting for you very much.’ Oh, how happy I am! What is this? How happy I am!” Pierre said to himself.

XIX.

Nothing was now taking place in Pierre’s soul like what had taken place in it under similar circumstances during his courtship of Hélène.

He did not repeat, as he had then, with painful shame, the words he had spoken; he did not say to himself, “Oh, why did I not say that, and why, why did I then say, ‘I love you’?” Now, on the contrary, he repeated every word of hers and his own in his imagination, with every detail of her face and smile, and wanted neither to subtract nor to add anything: he wanted only to repeat it. There was now not a shadow of doubt as to whether what he had undertaken was good or bad. Only one terrible doubt sometimes came into his mind. Was all this not a dream? Had Princess Marya not been mistaken? Am I not too proud and self-confident? I believe; but suppose, as is bound to happen, Princess Marya tells her, and she smiles and replies: “How strange! He must be mistaken. Does he not know that he is a man, merely a man, while I?... I am something quite different, something higher.”

This was the only doubt that often came to Pierre. Nor did he now make any plans. The happiness before him seemed so incredible that once it came to pass, there could be nothing beyond it. Everything ended there.

A joyful, unexpected madness, of which Pierre had thought himself incapable, took possession of him. The whole meaning of life, not for him alone but for the entire world, seemed to him to lie solely in his love and in the possibility of her love for him. Sometimes all people seemed to him to be occupied with only one thing—his future happiness. It sometimes seemed to him that they were all rejoicing just as he himself was and were merely trying to conceal that joy by pretending to be occupied with other interests. In every word and movement he saw hints of his happiness. He often surprised the people he met with his significant, happy glances and smiles, expressive of a secret understanding. But when he realized that people might not know about his happiness, he pitied them with all his heart and felt a desire somehow to explain to them that everything occupying them was utter nonsense and trifles unworthy of attention.

When he was offered a position in the service, or when some general affairs of state and the war were discussed on the assumption that the happiness of all people depended on one outcome or another, he listened with a gentle, commiserating smile and surprised those who spoke with him by his strange remarks. But both those people who seemed to Pierre to understand the true meaning of life—that is, his feeling—and those unfortunate people who obviously did not understand it—all people during this period appeared to him in such a bright light from the feeling shining within him that, without the slightest effort, the moment he met anyone at all, he saw in him everything that was good and worthy of love.

When he looked through the affairs and papers of his late wife, he felt no emotion toward her memory except pity that she had not known the happiness he now knew. Prince Vasili, particularly proud now of having received a new appointment and a star, seemed to him a touching, kind, and pitiful old man.

Pierre often recalled afterward this time of happy madness. All the judgments he formed about people and circumstances during this period remained forever true for him. Not only did he not later renounce these views of people and things, but, on the contrary, in moments of inner doubt and contradiction he had recourse to the view he had held during this time of madness, and that view always proved correct.
